title: College Openings Reading List
lens: For CJ's project on community and technical college openings and their effects on local firms, industry mix and innovation.

questions.text: Does an opening shift local establishments, sector employment or wages toward the fields the college teaches?
Does an opening raise local patenting or firm R&D, and is that plausible for teaching-focused 2-year colleges?
How do you build a counterfactual for a sited institution: runner-up sites, similar-criteria siting, synthetic control, distance rings, or funding shocks?
Which channel is it: skill supply, knowledge transfer, or local demand from the campus itself?

roles.benchmark: Closest analog result to compare against
roles.measurement: How to build an outcome or exposure

gap: No paper found on modern US community college openings with firm, establishment or patent outcomes (search of 2026-11-23). Bleemer & Quincy (2026) is the closest, for 1910s-1920s junior colleges.

papers.full: Junior Colleges and Local Development
papers.why: The only paper found on 2-year (junior college) openings with manufacturing, sector-mix and patent outcomes. Patenting is a null, which is itself the benchmark.

facts.design: Staggered DiD on ~300 openings, same-state comparison places
facts.data: Census microdata 1900-1940, Census of Manufactures and Agriculture

papers.abstract: The paper asks how local human capital affects regional productivity and spatial structural transformation. It studies the first wave of American two-year "junior" colleges, using the timing and location of every opening between 1900 and 1950 (p. 2). papers.full: The Effect of Postsecondary Educational Institutions on Local Economies: A Bird's-Eye View
papers.why: Modern US branch-campus openings, with employment in the sectors aligned to each campus's programs. This is the program-to-industry alignment outcome the project needs.

facts.data: Daytime satellite imagery; employment by sector

papers.abstract: The paper asks whether opening a postsecondary branch campus raises local economic activity, a question the authors say lacks evidence because data at a fine enough geography and long enough horizon are scarce (pp. 4–5). papers.why: The runner-up-site design for college establishment, with patents as the outcome. The hosted PDF is the 2018 draft, whose numbers differ from the published version.

facts.design: DiD against runner-up sites from site-selection histories

papers.abstract: The paper asks whether establishing a college causes local invention, whether colleges are necessary for it, and through what channel. papers.full: Innovation Effects of Universities of Applied Sciences: An Assessment of Regional Heterogeneity
papers.why: Swiss universities of applied sciences are the closest European analog to technical colleges. Patent effects are split by labor-market size, density and high-tech intensity.

facts.design: DiD on municipalities within 25 km of a new UAS campus

papers.abstract: Earlier studies of new higher education institutions report average patent increases of 7 to 32 percent, mostly for academic universities (p. 2). This paper asks whether the innovation effect of Swiss universities of applied sciences (UASs), bachelor-granting three-year colleges that teach and conduct applied research, varies with a region's economic preconditions (p. 1). papers.why: Firm R&D staffing after UAS openings, a direct firm outcome for an applied-college shock. No hosted PDF; an open working-paper copy is linked.

papers.full: University Innovation and Local Economic Growth
papers.why: Matches industries to a university's technical strengths. It is a template for measuring how closely a college's programs fit local industries.

papers.full: Do Universities Improve Local Economic Resilience?
papers.why: Similar site-selection criteria give the counterfactual (normal schools vs. insane asylums). This kind of design could carry over to 2-year college siting.

facts.design: Normal-school vs asylum counties, shift-share shocks

papers.abstract: The paper asks whether a regional (non-research-intensive) public university makes a local economy more resilient to adverse shocks, chiefly manufacturing decline (p. 1). It contributes in two ways (p. 2). First, it studies resilience, which the university-growth literature had not examined. Second, it proposes a new identification strategy: states placed normal schools (teacher training) and insane asylums in 1830–1

papers.full: Small Distances that Matter: Effects of Local Community College Openings on Enrollment and Degree Completion
papers.why: Modern Texas community-college openings, using distance rings and an imputation event study. The outcomes are enrollment only, but the design transfers directly.

facts.design: Event study, 20-minute vs 20-40-minute rings, BJS imputation

papers.full: Do Local Conditions Determine the Direction of Science? Evidence from U.S. Land Grant Colleges
papers.why: Shows whether colleges direct their research toward local crops. This is the analog of community colleges tailoring programs to local industry.

facts.design: Publication mix vs local crop mix

papers.abstract: The paper asks whether local conditions determine the direction of science, using agricultural research at U.S. land grant colleges (p. 1). papers.full: Regional Innovation Effects of Applied Research Institutions
papers.why: The Swiss UAS patent paper that the 2022 heterogeneity paper builds on. No hosted PDF; an open working-paper copy is linked.

papers.full: Education and Invention
papers.why: Finnish technical-university openings serve as an instrument for engineering education, with patents as the outcome. It is the skill-supply channel to innovation. No hosted PDF.

facts.design: IV: distance to new technical universities

papers.full: Local University Expansion and Firm Innovation: Evidence from Skilled Labor Supply Shocks and Innovation Efficiency
papers.why: Firm-level patents after Chinese university openings, with junior and vocational colleges as a comparison where effects are small or null. No hosted PDF.

papers.full: Universities as Engines for Regional Growth? Using the Synthetic Control Method to Analyze the Effects of Research Universities
papers.why: Synthetic control for upgrades of Swedish colleges to university status, with small and imprecise effects. It shows how limited inference is with few treated units.
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether granting research-university status to existing institutions raises regional output and entrepreneurship. The treatment is the 1999 Swedish university reform, which upgraded three university colleges (Karlstad, Örebro, Växjö) to universities with the right to award PhDs and with higher block research funding (pp. 1–3). papers.why: An endowment-shock IV for university spending, which separates spending (demand) from spillovers. It offers a template for funding-shock designs at community colleges.

facts.design: IV: stock-market shocks x lagged endowment

papers.abstract: The paper estimates the causal effect of research university activity on wages paid by local firms outside higher education (p. 1–2). papers.why: A synthetic control for a single opening. Its gains are mainly in nontraded services, which points to the local-demand channel.
papers.abstract: Lee (2018) asks whether opening a large research university raises local employment in the short run. The setting is the 2005 opening of UC Merced, which the paper describes as the first American research university built in the 21st century (p. 2). papers.why: Land-grant counties compared with matched synthetic-control counties, tracking long-run population and manufacturing share.
papers.abstract: The paper estimates short- and long-run effects of universities on geographic clustering of economic activity, labor market composition and local productivity, and interprets a productivity effect in a non-education sector as evidence of local spillovers (abstract, p. 1).
